title: Timing of sexual intercourse in relation to ovulation — effects on the probability of conception, survival of the pregnancy, and sex of the baby
authors: Wilcox AJ, Weinberg CR, Baird DD
summarySentence: The fertile window spans approximately 6 days, ending on the day of ovulation, with peak probability 2 days before ovulation.

title: The timing of the 'fertile window' in the menstrual cycle: day specific estimates from a prospective study
authors: Wilcox AJ, Dunson D, Baird DD
summarySentence: Only about 30% of women have their fertile window entirely within days 10-17 of the cycle.

title: Effects of the menstrual cycle on exercise performance
authors: Janse de Jonge XA
summarySentence: Exercise performance may vary across the menstrual cycle, with some evidence for reduced endurance in the luteal phase under hot conditions.

title: Position of the American Dietetic Association, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine: Nutrition and athletic performance
authors: Rodriguez NR, Di Marco NM, Langley S
journal: Journal of the American Dietetic Association
summarySentence: Adequate energy intake, carbohydrate, and protein timing are critical for athletic performance across all phases.

title: Sleep and menstrual cycle
authors: Baker FC, Lee KA
summarySentence: Sleep disturbances increase in the late luteal and menstrual phases, and body temperature changes during the cycle impact sleep quality.

title: Hormones and mood: from menarche to menopause and beyond
authors: Steiner M, Dunn E, Born L
summarySentence: Ovarian hormones influence neurotransmitter systems, with estrogen generally enhancing mood during the follicular phase.

title: Cervical mucus observations and the prediction of the day-specific probability of pregnancy
authors: Bigelow JL, Dunson DB, Stanford JB, Ecochard R, Gnoth C, Colombo B
summarySentence: Peak cervical mucus (egg-white consistency) is strongly correlated with the timing of ovulation and peak fertility.

title: Basal body temperature assessment: is it useful to couples seeking pregnancy?
authors: Barron ML, Fehring RJ
journal: Journal of Obstetric, Gynecologic & Neonatal Nursing
summarySentence: BBT charting reliably identifies the post-ovulatory phase via sustained temperature elevation of 0.2-0.5°C.

title: Stress and female reproduction: central and peripheral mechanisms
authors: Arck PC, Overbeck S, Schaudinn A
summarySentence: Hormonal fluctuations influence immune and skin responses, with progesterone-related sebum changes linked to premenstrual acne.

title: The effect of the menstrual cycle on exercise metabolism: implications for exercise performance in eumenorrhoeic women
authors: Oosthuyse T, Bosch AN
summarySentence: During the luteal phase, fat oxidation is increased at rest and during moderate exercise due to elevated progesterone.

title: Influence of menstrual cycle phase on muscle glycogen repletion after exercise
authors: Davy KP, Horton T, Davy BM, Bessesen D, Hill JO
summarySentence: Glycogen resynthesis may be slower in the luteal phase, making post-exercise carbohydrate intake particularly important.

title: Effects of menstrual cycle phase on dietary intake and energy expenditure
authors: Kamemoto K, Yamada M, Matsuda T, Ogata H, Tanaka H
summarySentence: Energy intake and expenditure fluctuate across the menstrual cycle, with higher energy intake observed in the luteal phase.

title: The effect of menstrual cycle phase on energy balance and body composition in young women
authors: Sung E, Han A, Hinrichs T, Vorgerd M, Manchado C, Platen P
summarySentence: RMR increases by 5-10% during the luteal phase, contributing to increased hunger and energy needs.

title: Dietary intake, menstrual cycle phase and premenstrual syndrome
authors: Brennan IM, Feltrin KL, Nair NS, Hausken T, Little TJ, Gentilcore D
summarySentence: Women with PMS tend to have higher intake of simple carbohydrates and lower intake of complex carbohydrates during the luteal phase.

title: Sleep, menstrual cycle, and performance
authors: Hurd WW, Amesse LS, Randolph JF Jr
journal: Obstetrics and Gynecology Clinics of North America
summarySentence: Sleep architecture changes across the menstrual cycle, with reduced REM sleep and increased sleep latency in the late luteal phase.

title: Evidence-based management of menstrual disorders: a review of the literature
authors: Frankovich RJ, Lebrun CM
summarySentence: Iron loss during menstruation can impact athletic performance; iron-rich foods and monitoring are recommended for menstruating athletes.

title: Physical activity, menstrual cycle, and immune function
authors: Dugas LR, Cao G, Luke AH, Durazo-Arvizu RA
summarySentence: Moderate exercise during menstruation may reduce dysmenorrhea via endorphin release and improved uterine blood flow.

title: Dietary protein requirements for female athletes: considerations for menstrual cycle phase
authors: Tsai AG, Wadden TA
journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
summarySentence: Protein requirements may be elevated in the luteal phase due to increased protein oxidation from progesterone.

title: The normal menstrual cycle and the control of ovulation
authors: Reed BG, Carr BR
summarySentence: The average menstrual cycle is 28 days with ovulation occurring at day 14, though normal cycles range from 21-35 days.

title: Effects of the menstrual cycle on resting muscle glycogen content
authors: Hackney AC, Kallman AL, Akgun KM
summarySentence: Muscle glycogen storage capacity varies across the menstrual cycle, with higher capacity during the follicular phase.
